content: An enzyme found in compost broke down small amounts of polyurethane foam in laboratory tests, offering an early lead toward gentler ways to recycle a stubborn plastic. The polyurethane used in mattress foam, shoe soles, and refrigerator insulation is notoriously difficult to recycle on an industrial scale. A very large share of the millions of metric tons produced worldwide ends up in landfills or incinerators, taking potentially reusable material with it. Nylon presents a similar challenge. Used in clothing, bags, cars, ropes, engine components, and fishing nets, it is another plastic made from crude oil, a finite resource. Researchers want to break both materials down into their pure components so those ingredients can become new polyurethane and nylon. Chemical and biological approaches are making progress, but the solutions emerging from laboratories are not yet ready for industrial use. Researchers from Aarhus University and the Danish Technological Institute went looking for help among bacteria. Their search took in a Kenyan landfill, a tropical zoo, the guts of wax moth larvae, and a compost heap near Aarhus. The best candidate came from the compost, where a bacterium produced an enzyme with an ability that could prove useful far beyond the heap. Researchers collected bacteria from plastic-contaminated environments, including a tropical zoo, a landfill in Kenya, compost and larval guts. Using fluorescent probes and fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), they isolated bacteria capable of cleaving chemical bonds found in polyurethane and nylon. The active enzymes were then purified and identified using chromatography, activity assays and mass spectrometry. In total, the researchers identified 10 polyurethane-degrading enzymes and 2 nylon-degrading enzymes. Credit: Rosie Graham / Angewandte Chemie Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. To find ones that can break down plastic, researchers conventionally search genome databases for gene sequences resembling those of enzymes already known to do the job. That approach has yielded useful enzymes, but there are relatively few known examples to guide the search. This team used bioprospecting, which means searching nature for organisms and genetic material that could be useful in research or industry. It was the first time researchers had searched on such a large scale and across such varied environments for enzymes capable of degrading polyurethane, also called PUR, and nylon. The idea came to Andreas Møllebjerg as he prepared to begin a postdoctoral position at what was then the Interdisciplinary Nano Science Center (iNANO) at Aarhus University. He was joining a new project investigating whether natural enzymes could break down plastic. Møllebjerg, a co-author of the resulting study, recently published in Angewandte Chemie , was responsible for collecting bacteria from different environments. “I suggested looking for suitable enzymes in places where it is warm, because bacteria thrive and grow well there all year round. And preferably somewhere plastic has been present for a long time. A year and a half later, I was on a plane to Kenya, followed by half an hour on the back of a local student’s motorbike on the way to a huge landfill. He helped me collect samples and communicate with the hundreds of people who lived on and off the landfill,” he says. Møllebjerg and PhD student and co-author Malthe Kjær Bendtsen also traveled 34 kilometers, about 21 miles, to collect plastic waste at Randers Regnskov Tropical Zoo. Møllebjerg bought a bag of wax moth larvae from a pet food shop so the team could investigate enzymes from bacteria in their guts. At a recycling center about 10 kilometers, or 6 miles, from the university, he collected a shovelful of compost. Those samples gave the researchers millions of bacteria to examine. Finding a useful enzyme required more than showing that a bacterium could react with a convenient laboratory substitute for plastic. “It was like a three-stage rocket, where we gradually narrowed them down. We started by finding bacteria that could break down the fluorescent model material. Then we isolated the enzymes capable of breaking down exactly that fluorescent material. And finally, we tested the enzymes on increasingly realistic materials,” Bendtsen explains. This 90-hour time-lapse video shows enzymatic degradation of two different molecules that mimic nylon. The second and fourth vials show CCPUR1 breaking down the two molecules, while the first and third vials show an inactive enzyme. Credit: Samuel Peña Díaz, Aarhus University, and Andreas Sommerfeldt, Danish Technological Institute For the initial screening, the researchers mixed bacteria with molecules designed to mimic chemical bonds in polyurethane and nylon. The molecules lit up when they encountered a bacterium containing a suitable enzyme. Using fluorescence-activated cell sorting, or FACS, a machine could screen the bacteria and pick out glowing cells at a rate of up to 10,000 per second. The search identified 29 plastic-degrading bacteria and 12 enzymes with varying abilities to break down polyurethane and nylon. The most promising enzyme was CC PUR1 , from the compost bacterium Chelatococcus composti . Its name takes “CC” from the bacterium and “PUR” from PURase, shorthand for polyurethane hydrolase, an enzyme capable of breaking down polyurethane. Testing on more realistic materials showed both its potential and its limitations. Given polyurethane mattress foam in powdered form, CC PUR1 broke down just under 1% in three days. That leaves a substantial gap between detecting an enzyme’s activity and using it to recycle plastic on an industrial scale. CC PUR1 nevertheless had several useful characteristics. Its unusually wide binding cleft, a groove where it accommodates the material it acts on, gives large polymer molecules room to fit. Polymers are the long molecules that make up plastics. The enzyme was also particularly stable, withstanding higher temperatures and a range of solvents better than the other candidates. Its origins in compost offer an explanation for those abilities. Compost contains stubborn plant materials such as wax and lignin, and an enzyme that evolved to break down those substances can also happen to work on plastic. Compost heaps can reach 80°C, or 176°F, so enzymes functioning there need enough stability to withstand the heat. The team has since worked to improve CC PUR1 . In a follow-up study published September 11, 2026, in Chem Catalysis , the researchers collaborated with the University of Porto, using computer simulations and targeted edits to the DNA instructions for making the enzyme. Within three days, the modified enzyme broke down around 1.4% of the polyurethane in foam from a real shoe sole, without any pretreatment of the plastic. That experiment used a different material from the powdered mattress foam in the original study. Postdoctoral researcher Rosie Graham, who was responsible for testing the enzymes on plastic materials in the laboratory, is the first author of the follow-up study. The other 11 enzymes could also have a role. They work best on small pieces of plastic and may complement CC PUR1 in future combinations of processes. Because enzymes are selective about what they act on, the researchers envisage using an enzyme cocktail in stages. Polyurethane could first be broken down and washed away, followed by the addition of nylon-degrading enzymes. Chemical methods cannot separate those tasks in the same way. Making these processes practical may require mechanical and chemical treatments that make the plastic easier for enzymes to attack. Chemical degradation of polyurethane and nylon is itself a major research field, including at Aarhus University. The scale of the remaining challenge is one reason the team compares efficient polyurethane recycling to finding the holy grail. “But the research highlights the strength of enzymes. Their real advantage when it comes to recycling is that they work under mild conditions, meaning at lower temperatures and pressures than those used in most recycling technologies today,” Graham says. Reference: “Environmental Identification of Novel Enzymes for Polyurethane and Polyamide Degradation” by Malthe Kjær Bendtsen, Andreas Møllebjerg, Samuel Peña-Díaz, Rosie Graham, Nicolai Claus Petersen, Bjørk Nolsøe Isaksen, Mathias Carstensen, Martin B. Johansen, Andreas Sommerfeldt, Allan R. Petersen, Iddi Khamisi Chuma, Cecilie Ryberg, Thomas Rea Wittenborn, Virginia Gichuru, Huabing Wang, Carsten Scavenius, Alexander Sandahl and Daniel E. Otzen, 26 June 2026, Angewandte Chemie International Edition . DOI: 10.1002/anie.6159643 This work is supported by the Novo Nordisk Foundation through the Challenge Grant NNF22OC0072891 to the Center EnZync. title: Ice-covered oceans and bleak craters: Where alien life might be hiding
content:
If life exists elsewhere, it might not be on worlds like Earth. Here are some of the more peculiar places scientists are looking.
So far, the search for life beyond Earth has broadly focused on worlds like our own.
We have considered potentially habitable planets that might have land and water , are the right distance from their star to have temperatures similar to those found on Earth, and are around stars similar to the Sun. Life might even be found in the moons that orbit our near neighbours, like Mars or Jupiter.
But what if life exists in stranger locations than we expected?
Increasingly, scientists are exploring unusual places where alien life might exist, and sometimes looking for it in peculiar ways. From trapped oceans to spotting the patterns of star-hopping extraterrestrials, there is an increasing diversity of ideas.
"We have our eyes open and are thinking about different kinds of life signatures we could look for," says Lisa Kaltenegger, an astrobiologist at Cornell University in the US and author of the book Alien Earths . "We are pushing the possibilities to not miss signs of life."
All life on Earth has several common requirements . Every organism we know of needs liquid water and a source of energy – sunlight for plants, and food for animals. They are also all made of carbon: without it, simple or complex life on our planet wouldn't exist. But this might not all be true everywhere else.
One place already showing an unexpected potential for life is Venus. In 2020, astronomers announced hints of a gas called phosphine in its atmosphere. While this can be produced by processes such as volcanic eruptions (and its existence on Venus in any case remains contested ), it can also be produced by life.
"We certainly did not expect" that Venus could have life, says Dave Clements, an astronomer at Imperial College London, although the idea was first touted back in the 1960s by the famous author and scientist Carl Sagan.
Venus seems an unusual place for life at first given that its surface can reach more than 400C (750F) and the pressure from the thick atmosphere is equivalent to standing at the bottom of Earth's oceans. About 55 to 65km (34 to 40 miles) above the surface of Venus, however, temperatures and pressures are the most Earth-like of any location in the solar system outside of our own world. It is here scientists think life could exist, as microbes floating in droplets among the clouds, burping out phosphine.
To find out more, several potential missions to Venus are planned. Clements is part of a UK-led mission called Verve (Venus Explorer for Reduced Vapours in the Environment), a small shoebox-sized spacecraft that Clements' team hopes will hitch a ride to Venus on an upcoming European mission called Envision, set to launch in 2031.
Once it arrived at Venus, Verve would detach and enter into a looping, elliptical orbit from far above the planet down much closer to its atmosphere.
Here, Verve would probe the atmosphere of Venus for signs of phosphine, and life. It would have "a receiver specifically tuned to the wavelengths we are interested in", says Clements, phosphine being one but also ammonia and hydrogen. Taken together, these readings could give us hints that there is life floating in the atmosphere, or not.
"This is not going to be a shaking-hands-with-little-green-men-type discovery of alien life," says Clements. "It's building the evidence for a case."
The Verve team is waiting to hear if they have been included on the Envision mission, a decision that will be made by the European Space Agency (Esa).
Another mission to Venus called Morning Star , from the US company Rocket Lab and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, will launch a probe to Venus as soon as this year. It aims to dive into its atmosphere and look for a possible signature of life through a technique called fluorescence.
"Most people agree the frontrunners are Mars and Europa" to find life, says Clements. "But maybe the outside bet is Venus."
Elsewhere in the Solar System, the dwarf planet Ceres is another unexpected location now being probed for life.
Found in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, this world is small, four times smaller than our Moon, and has a greyish, lifeless appearance. But when it was orbited by Nasa's Dawn spacecraft from 2015 to 2018, scientists discovered something strange on its surface: bright spots that seemed to be some sort of salty, brine-like substance.
In August 2025, Sam Courville at Arizona State University in the US proposed that Ceres might have been habitable in its past , a surprising suggestion for a world that seems very dead to human eyes. He suggested the world could have had an ocean under its surface with a steady supply of heat, providing key requirements for life to emerge. And the bright spots today might be the remnants of that ocean seeping out from underground.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a substantive scientific discovery, specifically the search for life in unusual places, such as Venus, and the consideration of alternative life signatures. It provides a clear reason for readers to care, highlighting the possibility of finding life beyond Earth and the potential for life existing in unexpected locations.

title: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
content: Cisco shares rose in extended trading on Thursday after the maker of networking gear reported better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results. Here's how the company did compared to LSEG consensus estimates: Revenue increased 24% from $14.88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement. Net income rose to $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share, from $2.9 billion, or 72 center per share, a year ago. Cisco is trying to gain a foothold in the artificial intelligence buildout after missing out on the early years of the generative AI boom. The company's stock price is up about 35% this year as of Thursday's close, trouncing the Nasdaq, which has gained 9% over that stretch. Cisco raised its expectation for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to $9 billion this fiscal year, more than double the figure in fiscal 2026. "Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era," CEO Chuck Robbins said in the statement . For the fiscal second quarter, Cisco said it expects revenue of between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, topping the average analyst estimate of $17.88 billion, according to LSEG. The company is projecting adjusted earnings per share of $1.34 to $1.36, beating the $1.23 average estimate.
